storyline.arc: It began in early June with a tmux-style terminal that only knew how to talk to Claude, and within a day that was torn open to speak OpenCode too. From there came multi-session support, sandboxing, session sharing over git, a rename, and a long stretch of making Windows a first-class citizen instead of an afterthought. Today it has a dashboard, a VS Code extension, an MSI pipeline, and a pre-commit guard that tells the agent no.

chapters.detail: Watching an agent work through a plain log is fine until you want to actually type back at it, so f207887 dropped in a tmux-like embedded terminal in one 1135-line push. Then came the awkward part: the whole session-reading layer assumed Claude, and ced9b84 tore it apart into a backend-shaped thing, with tests/test_opencode_parse.py and tests/test_opencode_session.py appearing alongside test_claude_session.py as proof. After that the pieces fell fast: session switching in b52b580, and aa0b2dc adding a check for whether the backend you asked for is even installed.

chapters.detail: The want was simple: run more than one session at a time without them stepping on each other. That landed across a run of commits, from the initial multi-session support through branch management across sessions and a scrolling fix, roughly 5000 lines in total. Then someone tried to start aGiT in a freshly `git init`ed folder with nothing in it, and it just refused to start. The fix was tiny by comparison, about 100 lines, and came with tests across test_worktree.py, test_state.py and test_cli.py so the empty-directory case stays covered.

chapters.detail: Publishing a release by hand is fine right up until branch protection tells you no, which is exactly what happened: scripts/publish.sh tried to merge straight into main and got bounced, so it was reworked to open a PR instead, and the same lesson had to be learned all over again for the new release-patch.yml and release-tag.yml workflows. Along the way the version number turned out to live in two hand-maintained places at once, so that got collapsed into a single source to stop aGiT reporting a version it wasn't actually running. The dashboard grew an activity-over-time chart with togglable series, x-axis zoom, and then a SHOW dropdown because dragging a chart to find last week is nobody's idea of fun. End result: v0.0.2 shipped through a pipeline instead of through willpower.
chapters.summary: A dashboard appeared alongside an auto-updater, and then two full days went into automated release workflows so shipping to PyPI and GitHub Releases stopped being a manual chore.

chapters.detail: The want was simple: hand a teammate a whole Claude session over git instead of a wall of copy-pasted transcript. Issue #55 got built, and then the questions started rolling in fast: how do I even know it shared, does it keep updating, why is my own shared session missing from the dashboard, and why did opening "Manage shared sessions" turn the terminal into treacle. That last one led to the auto-share being pulled off its own background timer and pinned to commit time instead, so GitHub does not get hammered, plus forced deletion of old session versions rather than waiting on git garbage collection. By the end you could bounce a session between two machines and swap sides, and OpenCode got the same export/import path.
chapters.summary: Full agent sessions became something you could share via git, and OpenCode got the same export/import treatment right after.

chapters.detail: Three days running, the same complaint landed in the prompts: sharing from machine B, then resuming on machine A, and machine A just shrugged and kept its own old copy. The fix went deep into tests/test_session_sharing.py, moving session identity to GitHub id with contributor sets so "my session" actually means the same thing on both machines, and bdd8bc9 made the resume worker stop handing back the stale local version. chapters.detail: The want was simple to say and messy to build: run several sessions at once on different branches without touching the base branch in the repo directory. That turned into a per-session merge branch (a621a5e), a branch picker at session creation with off-branch names bolded in the status bar, and a guard that warns before merging across branches instead of waiting for a conflict to explain itself. Along the way the git-base-branch option got asked out of existence, and the dashboard screenshot had to be retaken twice: once because the path still said agit, once because it was leaking a home directory path in public.
chapters.summary: The rename shipped complete with screenshots and publishing, and the merge branch was split per session so concurrent work would stop stepping on itself.

thoughts.note: Working out that concurrent sessions need their own merge target, with the base branch as the safe default.
thoughts.quote: I'd like to allow concurrent sessions on independent branches, without having to change the base branch in the repo directory. The user can select whether to apply merge changes to the base branch (default option) or to a different branch. When merging into a different branch than the one the repo's main directory is checked out, the status bar should emphasize that the branch the changes will be merged into is not the one on the directory. The emphasis may change if the user changes the branch on the repo directory.

thoughts.note: Realizing the intro-page screenshot was about to publish their home directory path, so ~ abbreviation came first and the reshoot second.
thoughts.quote: When the repo is a subfolder in the home folder, use ~ in the path instead of the full path in the dashboard. Once implemented, redo the dashboard screenshot for the intro page, since the home directory path should not be shared in public. In addition, the label "aGiTrack-tracked AI" is cumbersome; just say "Tracked AI" instead.

chapters.detail: The original ask was pure battery politics: stop burning CPU when nobody has touched the aGiTrack terminal and no session is running. After that the scope quietly exploded into learn.py and a full learning page with step-by-step lessons, tooltips explaining what "gaps closed" actually means, and a skip button that finally does something; along the way the dashboard screenshot got retaken twice, once after a background task ran for an hour before anyone noticed something was wrong.

chapters.detail: The complaint was very specific: running in no-worktree mode, aGiTrack kept popping up its commit dialog asking to commit edits that a background task had made, not the developer. First attempt tried to attribute files to an author, and the developer shot down both anchors in a row, first directories as unreliable, then exact paths because the user and a background task can touch the same file anyway. chapters.detail: It started with a very reasonable question: the agent kept hitting write errors mid-edit, and the developer asked whether it was because they were coding aGiTrack inside aGiTrack. Basically yes, so an atomic write helper went into agitrack/metrics/daemon.py and friends, and the daemons stopped being terminal-owned so the Ctrl-G dashboard behaves exactly like agitrack -d. The best part came later: an auto-restart-after-update landed, and then both dashboards promptly stopped, which forced the swap from exec-based restart to spawn-and-verify with rollback, plus keeping failed daemons visible under -daemons instead of quietly vanishing.
chapters.summary: Concurrent writes were corrupting files while the agent edited the very tool watching it, so an atomic write helper landed, and daemons were reworked to run free-standing and retry after a failed restart.

chapters.detail: The bug was almost comedic: paste a block of code into the backend agent's terminal and every line break got read as a fresh Enter keypress, which then went and answered aGiTrack's own pop-up about new commits for you. The fix landed in agitrack/proxy/modal.py and runner.py so pasted newlines stop reaching the modal dialogs, and the same push brought agitrack/update/selfupdate.py with a lock so several running instances don't try to update over each other. After that a paste is just a paste, and updating no longer depends on you having only one aGiTrack open.
chapters.summary: Multi-line pastes into the backend agent's terminal were eating line breaks, and the same push shipped self-update that survives multiple instances running at once by locking.

thoughts.note: Working out that a pasted line break and a real Enter key look identical to the UI, and that only the modal needs to care about the difference.
thoughts.quote: When pasting multiple lines into the backend agent's terminal, some line breaks in what is pasted gets detected by aGiTrack as Enter, which unintentionally gets applied to aGiTrack's pop up menu asking users about new commits etc. This should be avoided.

thoughts.note: Deciding that self-update can start from either the TUI or the daemon, which immediately means two of them could race.
thoughts.quote: aGiTrack should self-update when it can, which can be triggered by either the TUI or the daemon. There is no need to ask the user for updating the installation itself, although the TUI should not automatically restart to avoid interruptions (the same update restart reminder in the TUI should stay). When multiple aGiTrack instances are running, make sure their self-updates don't clash, so there needs to be some mechanism that only one aGiTrack instance can start a self-update, maybe through a lock mechanism.
